Worth it, though, for Manville on flying form as a rare bird of prey.
While its length is a problem, its high points are riveting, Herrin’s production is cool and stylish, and it’s worth the surfeit to see Manville at her resplendent best.
But his Kushner-isms ultimately get in the way of this play being as good as it could be.
Jeremy Herrin's three-and-a-half-hour production suffers from terminal bloat, it is undeniably blessed in its leading old lady, whom Manville shapes as a couture-crafted entity beyond good and evil.
In Kushner’s hands, however, Dürrenmatt’s brisk script mushrooms into a production that is almost four hours long with two intervals.
But for all its opulence, this self-indulgent show lacks heart and, at four hours, is far, far too long.
Lesley Manville is magnificent as a billionaire seeking revenge, but this cartoonish play misses the mark.

Herrin’s production expertly balances small-town detail with epic sweep, the division between the two punctuated by woozy ’50s jazz played live by a quintet, highlighted by Miles Davis-like muted trumpet.
But there's an awful lot of everything and when Manville is not centre stage, the action feels curiously airless.
But Manville’s whiplash-smart assuredness in a role that calls for a star and gets one proves one of the few invigorating aspects of a long and spirit-depleting evening.
Herrin's sumptuous production is a self-justifying exercise in theatrical spectacle.

cn.t: Manville delivers a commanding performance in Kushner's overlong adaptation of Dürrenmatt's tragicomedy. Critics praise the star turn and lavish production but consistently cite excessive length as a major flaw in this mixed reception.
